title: PL/pgSQL Functions
what_is_it: A function packages a calculation under a name with real parameters and a return type, callable from inside a query (SELECT my_func(...)). Its body is written in PL/pgSQL, Postgres's own procedural language, wrapped between $$ markers with BEGIN ... END; and using real control flow (IF/ELSIF/ELSE) and a RETURN statement.
why_it_matters: Some calculations are reused across many queries, or need real branching logic that a single SQL expression can't express cleanly - a function lets you write that logic once, name it, and call it anywhere a value is expected, the same way a Python function avoids repeating the same block of code.
common_mistakes: Forgetting that a function body needs its own END IF; to close an IF block, SEPARATE from the END; that closes the whole function - these are two different, independently-required closing keywords. Also writing RETURNS void (or forgetting RETURNS entirely) when the function is actually meant to hand back a computed value.
mini_exercise: Why does discounted_price(100, 20) return a NUMERIC with lots of trailing zeros (80.00000000000000000000) instead of a plain 80?
postgres_note: PL/pgSQL is one of several procedural languages Postgres supports for function bodies - PL/Python and PL/Perl also exist as optional extensions, but PL/pgSQL is the built-in default and by far the most common choice.
